Context: Set in `2014`, the current world record for running a marathon (`text(26.2 miles)`) is `text(two hours)`, `text(two minutes)`, and `text(57 seconds)`. Breaking2 is a scientific project to achieve a goal long thought to be impossible - running a marathon in under `text(two hours)`. In this passage, runner Ed Caesar describes his experience training with Olympic gold medalist Eliud Kipchoge, one of Breaking2's elite athletes.
Title: Passage 2: [from] “The Secret to Running a Faster Marathon? Slow Down”
Author: by Ed Caesar
Content: On `text(Wednesday, January 26)`, I ran `text(10 kilometers)` through a forest in Kaptagat, Kenya, with Eliud Kipchoge, a few of his friends, and some of the scientists from Nike's Breaking2 project. It was `text(4 pm)` and still blazing hot. We were at `text(8,000 feet)` of altitude...

The pace gently increased from around `text(5 minutes per kilometer)` to a little north of `text(4:40 per kilometer)`. All you could hear was the hi-hat beat of sneakers on dust and the straining bellows of an outsized mzungu¹ attempting to hang with the Olympic marathon champion...

Kipchoge has run whole marathons almost `text(twice)` as fast as we were moving at that moment. Why had he chosen not to crank up the pace? ... Kipchoge is polite to a fault. Was he simply humoring his guests? When we returned to his training camp, another possibility emerged. This was a recovery run, and Kipchoge really does take his recovery runs that slowly. The data the Nike science team analyzed from his GPS watch shows that the kind of run he had done with us was exactly the kind of run he would have done anyway...
I knew Kipchoge was fast. I didn't understand how slow he could be. This, I thought, might be a moment to learn something...

Nike has recently contracted a garrulous Chicago physician named Phil Skiba, who has trained many elite endurance athletes, to work on Breaking2. Skiba has developed algorithms that accurately measure and predict training loads. He is particularly interested by fatigue, and the balance between what he calls the “positive and negative effects of training.” In particular, Skiba uses athletes' training data to predict when, before a race, they should begin their taper - that is, to progressively decrease their volume of training so that they arrive on race `text(day)` fresh and fast.

`text(Every athlete)` has a different taper point. Some people need only a few `text(days)`. Some people need `text(weeks)`. The variations are explained both by differences in workload and by our physiological differences. Some athletes simply recover quicker from hard training than others, in ways that geneticists and physiologists are still trying to fully understand. Skiba's data, however, is precise. He and the Breaking2 crew believe that Kipchoge's taper may have started a `text(day)` or `text(two)` lat before his previous marathons and that he would have benefitted from around a `text(week)` of rest rather than his normal `text(five days)`...

Watching Kipchoge's group at work, I saw that they never did `text(two)` intense days back to back; they were always committed to developing their fitness, in the Kenyan parlance, “slowly by slowly.” Patrick Sang, Kipchoge's coach and a formidable presence in the athlete's life, explained to me the basis of this philosophy as he stood at the side of the track with a stopwatch in his hand and his red-and-black hoodie fastened tightly around his head. Our conversation had begun when I asked Sang why Kipchoge's group were doing a `text(12 x 1,200-meter)` session on that `text(day)`.

Sang said this session was to build “speed-endurance” - the ability to maintain a high speed for a long time. But if you thought about only `text(one)` workout, you missed the point. The idea of a training program, Sang told me, was to improve `text(every aspect)` of a runner. The approach was holistic. If you scheduled a speed-endurance session for a `text(Tuesday)`, you needed to make sure that the following `text(day)` would be light, so that the guys had time to recover before the `text(Thursday)` long run. `text(Friday)` would again be light, before a different kind of speed workout on `text(Saturday)`. `text(Sunday)` was a `text(day)` of rest. A good `text(day)` of training was worth little on its own, but a good `text(month)` was worth plenty. Slowly by slowly, the athlete's shape came. “`text(Every session)` is a building block,” Sang said.
